In 1912 , February 12 was the day the last-ever Emperor of China abdicated his throne after the Xinhai Revolution.Known as Puyi , or the Xuantong Emperor , the boy was aged just six years old when he was forced to relinquish his rule . <p> http : **40;7165;TOOLONG ... While Puyi was briefly restored to the throne as emperor by the warlord Zhang Xun from July 1 to 12 in 1917 , the boy leader was ultimately expelled from the Forbidden City in 1924 , abolishing his imperial title and privileges and reducing him to a private citizen of the Republic of China.From there , he moved to the country 's north-east and led a relatively vibrant political life , becoming the emperor of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo in 1932 , imprisoned as a war criminal after the establishment of the People 's Republic of China in 1949 and dying of kidney cancer and heart disease on 17 October 1967 , aged 61 . <p> http : **40;7207;TOOLONG ... In 2001 , February 11 was the day 20-year-old Dutch student Jan de Wit unleashed a computer worm onto the Internet designed to rapidly spread among users.Working under the alias ' OnTheFly ' , de Wit created and distributed the malicious program using the image of famous Russian tennis star Anna Kournikova and tricking millions of people and email servers around the world . <p> http : **40;7249;TOOLONG ... After de Wit sent the virus out via an online news group , the program arrived to its victims in an email with the subject line " Here you have , ; 0 ) " and an attached file called **26;7291;TOOLONG email itself never presented an actual image of Kournikova , but when people attempted to open the image file a virus program was launched that forwarded itself to everybody in their address books . <p> http : **40;7319;TOOLONG ... De Wit ultimately himself in to authorities in the town of Sneek after he had realised the rapid spread of the virus.In a letter posted online , he admitted to creating the worm and using Kournikova 's beauty to trick victims , also saying his motivations was to see whether the IT community had learned to improve their cyber security.The 20-year-old was eventually sentenced to just 150 hours of community service . <p> http : **40;7361;TOOLONG ... In 1845 , February 7 was the day the unique , priceless and irreplaceable Portland Vase - which had been exhibited in the UK 's British Museum in London - was shattered into ore than 80 pieces.The glass Roman vase , measuring 24.5cm high , was discovered in a funerary monument in Rome in the 16th century and thought to have dated back to the first Century BC . <p> http : **40;8747;TOOLONG ... On February 6 , 1938 a crowd of 35,000 people had flocked to Australia 's most famous beach when tragedy struck and Bondi 's lifesavers were left to handle a situation so dire it has forever been remembered as ' Black Sunday ' . In a freak event of nature , the waves at Bondi Beach that day began to roll in so frequently that a backwash so large was created that it began to sweep hundreds of unaware swimmers out to sea . <p> http : **40;8915;TOOLONG ... " There was instant panic . Men , women and children fighting for their lives , " the Bondi Surf Life Savers Club has said about the incident . " It was mass hysteria at its worst . In the frenzy they shouted , screamed , cried , begged and prayed . They grabbed , clawed and fought . " On the beach there was a stunned but short-lived silence . " <p> http : **40;8957;TOOLONG ... Lifesavers spread along the beach who were preparing for local swim competitions leaped into action and began to rescue and resuscitate as many swimmers as they could.Bondi 's surf clubhouse was instantly turned into a makeshift emergency ward where drowning swimmers were hurriedly taken , while more than 30 resuscitations happened on the beach itself.After 30 long minutes , 250 swimmers had needed help , 150 were rescued unharmed , 60 suffered immersion , 35 were rescued unconscious and revived and five people were tragically killed . <p> http : **40;8999;TOOLONG ... In 1994 - 31 years after the tragic and racially-fuelled shooting death of US civil rights leader and activist Medgar Evers - his family finally received justice for his killing.On February 5 , white supremacist and Ku Klux Klansman Byron De La Beckwith was finally convicted of his murder . <p> http : **40;9167;TOOLONG ... In 1977 , February 4 was the day of the Chicago Loop derailment disaster that was - at the time - the city 's worst-ever transit accident.In a bizarre set of circumstances , the incident saw four cars of a city train carriage launched off an escalated railway after jack-knifing before then plummeting to the ground below . <p> http : **40;9797;TOOLONG ... At about 5.25pm on February 4 , a Ravenswood train was waiting on the tracks , just past the northeast turn , waiting for another train to clear the platform of the State/Lake station.It was then that a third train began to move forward behind the Ravenswood service , against track and cab signals telling it to stop , making the two trains collide and begin to thrust up into the air off the tracks . <p> http : **40;9839;TOOLONG ... In 1976 , residents in the tiny Guatemalan town of Los Amates , north-east of Guatemala City , were woken in the early hours of the morning by a powerful earthquake that flattened entire buildings and shifted the country 's landscape.The 7.5-magnitude tremor first rocked the country at 03.01am on February 4 along the Motagua Fault and caused widespread damages . <p> http : **40;9923;TOOLONG ... The force of the earthquake saw entire houses simply fall away from their foundations after landslides were sparked in the chaos.With the earthquake also striking at such an early hour , many deaths were recorded because residents had been asleep when the damages began . <p> http : **40;9965;TOOLONG ... The most heavily affected area covered some 30,000 square kilometres , with a population of 2.5 million . Some 23,000 people were reported dead and 77,000 wounded.In rural areas , the force of the tremor was also so strong that rail tracks and infrastructure were physically moved or re-shaped in the quake . <p> http : **40;10007;TOOLONG ... In 1606 , January 31 was the day famous English Catholic anarchist Guy Fawkes died prematurely during his execution over the failed Gunpowder Treason Plot of the year before.A former Spanish fighter , Fawkes had generated popularity for a Catholic revolt in England against then-King James I. <p> http : **40;11267;TOOLONG ... The plotters - a group of English Catholics - leased a cellar space beneath the UK House of Lords , with the plan to blow it up from underneath during the State Opening of Parliament on November 5 , 1605 . Fawkes was placed in charge of the gunpowder which they stockpiled in the cellar , however the plot was revealed in an anonymous letter that directed authorities via a search to him while he was guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder -- enough to reduce the House of Lords to rubble . <p> http : **40;11309;TOOLONG ... After his arrest , Fawkes was sentenced to death by execution , hanging and then to be traditionally drawn and quartered on January 31 , 1606 . Despite that , through a conscious effort or not , Fawkes fell from the scaffold where he was to be hanged and broke his neck , thus avoiding the agony of being killed by the English government . <p> http : **40;11351;TOOLONG ... The entire Guy Fawkes story has forever since been etched into history as synonymous with anarchism and rebellion against authorities and governments.In the modern day , that has embodied itself in the Guy Fawkes masks protesters are seen wearing around the world to hide their identities while also making a statement about their opposition to ruling powers . <p> http : **40;11393;TOOLONG ... In 1937 , January 23 was the day of the second instalment of what came to be known as the Moscow Trials in Soviet Russia.The trials were a series of court hearings that were aimed at eliminating Soviet opposition.In this trial , 17 figureheads were put before a court accused of being anti-Soviet Trotskyists.Of those 17 , thirteen of the defendants were eventually executed by shooting after the trial , while the rest received sentences in labour camps . <p> http : **40;13871;TOOLONG ... Metesky often placed warning calls to the buildings where he had planted bombs , but would not specify the device 's exact location.Generally , they were gunpowder-filled pipe bombs , ranging in size and most used timers constructed from flashlight batteries and pocket watches . Metesky 's arrest ultimately came as a result of an early form of New York offender profiling , using clues given in letters he wrote to a newspaper.He was found legally insane and committed to a state mental hospital before he died on May 23 , 1994 aged 90 . <p> http : **40;13997;TOOLONG ... On January 22 , 2008 aged just 28 , Australian film icon Heath Ledger died as a result of a drug overdose in his apartment in New York City.Born in Perth , the young actor 's career spanned 19 different feature films - including hit titles such as ' 10 Things I Hate About You ' , ' A Knight 's Tale ' and ' Brokeback Mountain ' - and he had begun to develop a global fan following . <p> http : **40;14039;TOOLONG ... " <p> http : **40;14081;TOOLONG ... In 1984 , the world of computing changed forever on January 22 with the world introduction of the Macintosh computer in a television advert that aired during the third quarter of Super Bowl XVIII.The ad , titled " 1984 " , used an unnamed heroine to represent the coming of the Macintosh as a means of saving humanity from IBM 's attempts to dominate the computer industry.Two days later , the computer went on sale and by the end of the year purchases had boomed so much that Apple had expected to sell at least 250,000 units.That moment in global technology also spurred an entire line of Apple computers that have since revolutionised the industry . <p> http : **40;14207;TOOLONG ... In 1976 , the world 's first-ever supersonic passenger plane - the British and French , turbojet-powered Concorde - was introduced to the world for travel on January 21 . The aircraft had a maximum speed over twice the speed of sound at 2180km/h at cruise altitude and provided seating for up to 128 passengers.The Concorde was jointly developed and manufactured by Sud Aviation and the British Aircraft Corporation and was used mainly by wealthy passengers who could afford to pay a high price . <p> http : **40;14249;TOOLONG ... The Concorde flew regular transatlantic flights between London 's Heathrow Airport and Paris 's Charles de Gaulle Airport to John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York CIty , Washington Dulles International Airport in Virginia , and Grantley Adams International Airport in Barbados.It also flew these routes in less than half the time of other airliners . The aircraft was in operation for 27 years until 2003 when it was discontinued and in all that time there was just one fatal crash - that of Air France Flight 4590 on July 25 , 2000That plane erupted into flames after departing from Charles de Gaulle Airport , killing all 100 passengers and nine crew members on board and four people on the ground . <p> http : **40;14291;TOOLONG ... In 1968 , January 21 was also the date one of the most widely-publicised and controversial battles of the Vietnam War began - the Battle of Khe Sanh.In what was a forward push by the North Vietnamese People 's Army of Vietnam , US troops stationed at the Khe Sanh Combat Base , south of Hanoi , came under heavy fire after being surrounded.That push led to five months of intense combat that included artillery , mortar , and rocket attacks . <p> http : **40;14333;TOOLONG ... In response to the siege , the US Air Force launched an operation that saw 100,000 tons of bombs dropped and over 158,000 artillery rounds fired.That equated to 5000 bombs being dropped daily , exploding the same amount of land as five Hiroshima-sized atomic bombs . <p> http : **40;14375;TOOLONG ... The intense combat only came to an end on July 9 after a mission code-named Operation Pegasus that saw an influx of US military men come to the assistance of the surrounded troops.That move saw the US attempt to claim a victory in the battle , despite the Vietnamese also doing the same for having driven them out of the area.In total , just 274 US troops were killed in the battle and thousands more injured while up to eight-times more casualties than that were recorded for the Vietnamese Army . <p> http : **40;14417;TOOLONG ... In 1950 , January 17 was the day an 11-member robbery gang committed what was then deemed the " crime of the century " after breaking into a Brink 's security building in Boston and made away with US$2.7 million ( now valued at around $29.5m or AUD$42.7m ) . The historic theft left investigators confused , in part due to the low number of clues left behind in the security building 's vault . <p> http : **40;15509;TOOLONG ... It was later revealed that the robbers had managed to duplicate locks held within the building 's heavy doors and then , dressed in Brink 's uniforms , seven of the 11 entered the building posing as staff members.Within a 35-minute window , they had gagged multiple employees and forced them to handover money that had been counted . <p> http : **40;15551;TOOLONG ... In 1991 , the United States of America officially launched widespread military combat against Iraq with Operation Desert Storm , commonly known as the Gulf War.The war was waged by coalition forces comprised from 35 different nations , led by the US , and was sparked by Iraq 's invasion of Kuwait after lengthy oil pricing and production disputes . <p> http : **40;15719;TOOLONG ... From January 16 , 1991 onwards the USA 's combined forces subjected Iraq to 42 consecutive days and nights of bombings - one of the most intensive air bombardments in military history . The coalition flew over 100,000 sorties , dropped around 88,500 tons of bombs and widely destroyed Iraqi military and civilian infrastructure . <p> http : **40;15761;TOOLONG ... Bush.The coalition ceased its advance on Iraqi territories and declared a ceasefire 100 hours after the ground campaign started.Despite that , the USA and Kuwait suffered around 5000 fatalities during the combat and up to 50,000 Iraqis were killed in the war . <p> http : **40;15803;TOOLONG ... January 16 was also the day in 2003 that NASA 's historic Space Shuttle Columbia was launched on its tragic final-ever mission designed to conduct a series of scientific and atmospheric experiments.In its lifetime , Columbia served NASA for over 22 years and completed 27 missions before its final task was marred by disaster . <p> http : **40;15845;TOOLONG ... In 1947 , January 15 was the day the hideously mutilated remains of murdered American woman Elizabeth Short were found in a vacant lot in Los Angeles , sparking a police investigation that has since spanned seven decades.Since given the name ' Black Dahlia ' , Short 's heavily slashed , naked corpse was found severed in two at the waist , drained of blood , her face slashed from the mouth to her ears and her body " posed " , with her hands over her head , her elbows bent at right angles , and her legs spread apart . <p> http : **40;16013;TOOLONG ... Born in Boston , on the USA 's east coast , Short had moved to California as an aspiring actress , though she had no known acting credits or jobs during her time in Los Angeles.The Black Dahlia 's looks attracted the attention of media organisations and the public across the country and sparked widespread scrutiny of the case and of her character . <p> http : **40;16055;TOOLONG ... In 1967 , British paleoanthropologist and archaeologist Louis Leakey announced what he claimed to be the discovery of the oldest known ancestor of man - dating back some 20 million years.Leakey 's work throughout his career was seen as revolutionary in demonstrating that humans evolved in Africa . <p> http : **40;16307;TOOLONG ... The first significant fossil linked to the human form and attributed to Leakey was a robust skull with huge teeth dated to 1.75 million years ago.That discovery was unveiled by Louis ' collaborator and second wife Mary Leakey , and it was ultimately named ' Zinjanthropus boisei ' . <p> http : **40;16349;TOOLONG ... While some saw Leakey 's work in Africa and his discoveries as controversial , it is generally accepted that he radically changed the way early humans are seen through the scientific lens . His work pushed back the known dates for the existence of various human species , stimulated research in new fields like primatology - which also inspired the careers of famed researchers such as Jane Goodall - and generated interest and publicity for the study of human origins . <p> http : **40;16391;TOOLONG ... In 2016 , the world was shocked by the sudden and untimely death of one of the most influential musicians of the 20th century - David Bowie , who lost his battle with liver cancer at the age of 69 . Acclaimed by critics and musicians around the world for his innovative creations , Bowie became one of the best-selling musicians on the globe during his career and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1996 . <p> http : **40;17987;TOOLONG ... Bowie 's death came just two days after his 69th birthday - which was the day he also released his final-ever album ' Blackstar ' , and also after a lengthy battle with cancer.He had been diagnosed with the disease 18 months earlier but had not wanted the news of his illness made public.After the announcement of his death broke , murals and vigils around the world were created in his honour to showcase his music and multiple stages of his career - such as his ' Aladdin Sane ' persona seen here in his hometown of Brixotn , South London . <p> http : **40;18029;TOOLONG ... Following his death , Bowie 's producer Tony Visconti said that the musician had always : " did what he wanted to do . " " He wanted to do it his way and he wanted to do it the best way . His death was no different from his life -- a work of art , " he said at the time . " He made Blackstar for us , his parting gift . " He will always be with us . For now , it is appropriate to cry . " <p> http : **40;18071;TOOLONG ... Following his passing , sales of Bowie 's albums and singles worldwide skyrocketed.The musician , however , had always insisted that he did not want a funeral and so - after his cremation - his ashes were scattered in a Buddhist ceremony in Bali , Indonesia . <p> http : **40;18113;TOOLONG ... In 1920 , January 10 was the day that the Treaty of Versailles officially came into effect following the conclusion of World War I - finally confirming peace and the end of combat between Germany and the Allied Forces.The signing came following multiple meetings including representatives of the " Big Four " nations , or ( left to right ) : the UK 's David Lloyd George , Italy 's Vittorio Orlando , France 's Georges Clemenceau and the USA 's Woodrow Wilson.The Treaty has historically been seen as controversial , however , because - among its many provisions - one of the most significant inclusions was a requirement for Germany " to accept the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage " during the war.That single line in the Treaty meant that Germany had to disarm , give up large amounts of territory and pay reparations to certain countries estimated at a cost of 132 billion marks ( roughly AUD$618 billion in 2020 ) . <p> http : **40;18155;TOOLONG ... The Treaty was initially signed on June 28 the year before after six months of intense negotiations following the Armistice in the previous November , however it took another six months for it to come into effect around the world.The result of the period of tension and controversy - as well as competing and sometimes conflicting goals among the victors - was a compromise that left no one satisfied and Germany was neither pacified , conciliated or permanently weakened . <p> http : **40;18197;TOOLONG ... Eight hundred children were packed into the Laurier Palace Theatre in Montreal , Canada , on January 9 , 1927 , when a fire started.With the lights out and no exits marked , the children pushed against an inwards-opening door , with hundreds desperate to escape the smoke.Firefighters arrived from a station across the road , but were unable to get inside to save the children or extinguish the fire quickly . <p> http : **40;18239;TOOLONG ... In the end , 78 children died , including one from a fireman involved in the rescue , and three from a policeman.The tragedy became known as the " Saddest fire " . The cause of the fire was never discovered , but a discarded cigarette is often blamed . <p> http : **40;18281;TOOLONG ... The children were watching the Stan Laurel comedy Get ' Em Young.Grief in Montreal soon turned to anger , and Quebecois legislators soon banned children under 16 from attending cinemas.That law would not be overturned until 1961 . <p> http : **40;18323;TOOLONG ... One of the most notorious failures in military history , the Gallipoli campaign ended with a remarkable success.After more than nine months of bloodshed and stalemate , the decision was made to evacuate thousands of British , French and Anzac troops from the Turkish peninsula.But knowing that an evacuation could soon turn into a rout , it took extraordinary delicacy to slip away unnoticed . <p> http : **40;18365;TOOLONG ... More than 30,000 casualties were anticipated in the evacuation effort , but in the end , it was a tiny fraction of that.No Australians would be killed on the final night in Gallipoli.The final troops would leave the peninsula on January 9 , 1916 . <p> http : **40;18449;TOOLONG ... In 1981 , January 8 marked the historic date of the " Trans-en-Provence Case " , in which a French farmer is said to have seen an Unidentified Flying Object that left behind physical evidence on his property.At the scene , as depicted here in an artist 's impression drawn after the incident , 55-year-old Renato Nicola ? claimed to have heard a strange whistling sound about 5pm . He then said he saw a saucer-shaped object about two metres in diameter land about 46 metres away . <p> http : **40;18575;TOOLONG ... Nicola ? later told French space investigators that " the device had the shape of two saucers , one inverted on top of the other . " This device had a ridge all the way around its circumference . Under the machine I saw two kinds of pieces as it was lifting off . They could be reactors or feet , " he said . " There were also two other circles which looked like trapdoors . The two reactors , or feet , extended about 20cm below the body of the machine . " The farmer also said that the object took off almost immediately , but burn marks on the ground where it had supposedly sat - marked out here with the letters A , B and C. <p> http : **40;18617;TOOLONG ... French space investigators from a body known as GEPAN , soon arrived on the property and spoke to the farmer before taking soil samples to test his theory.The analysis of those samples showed that the ground had been flattened by a mechanical pressure of about four to five tonnes and heated to between 300 and 600C . Phosphate and zinc were also found in the samples , and chlorophyll levels were between 30 and 50 per cent lower than expected . <p> http : **40;18659;TOOLONG ... Investigators were told Nicola ? first thought the device was a secret military tool , because of his close living proximity to an army base.GEPAN never confirmed this was the case and the exact reasoning behind what the saucer-like object may have been has never been completely discovered.Despite that , media organisations at the time labelled the incident as " perhaps the most completely and carefully documented sighting of all time " . <p> http : **40;18701;TOOLONG ... In 1931 , Australian aviator Guy Menzies completed the world 's first-ever solo trans-Tasman flight from Sydney to the west coast of New Zealand in an Avro Sports Avian aircraft that had been first transported from England.The daring mission almost never happened after Menzies began to fear that he might be denied permission for the trip by air authorities.Before embarking , he decided to tell the authorities and his family that he was flying to Perth . <p> http : **40;18827;TOOLONG ... At 1am on January 7 however , Menzies flew out of Sydney on his own.The voyage took 11 hours and 45 minutes and his brave effort remains solidified in history solely for his landing into New Zealand - heavily affected by poor weather he crash-landed upside-down in the La Fontaine Swamp near Hari Hari on the nation 's western coastline . <p> http : **40;18869;TOOLONG ... Despite the landing , the Australian aviator smashed the previous record set for a trans-Tasman flight by Charles Kingsford Smith and Charles Ulm in 1928 by two-and-a-half hours.Later in life , he went on to become a squadron leader in World War II and was killed when his flying boat was shot down over the Mediterranean Sea . <p> http : **40;18911;TOOLONG ... @@71694982 <p> Sum up Australian politics in one short sentence , with particular reference to last year 's federal election . Economy beats climate change ? Leadership matters ? Queensland beats the rest ? My single sentence would be : old men beat young women . That 's my conclusion after reading Sarah Cameron and Ian McAllister 's The 2019 Australian Federal Election : Results from the Australian Election Study . It is a short booklet , reporting on the latest iteration of a survey series which began in 1987 . The section which contains the most stunning material is headed " A divided electorate ? " . From it I learnt that while geographical differences remain important , the revelations about the gender gap and the generational divide are more so . According to the Australian Election Study survey , the gender gap is widening and has reversed over time since the 1970s . It was Labor which used to have a " woman problem " . Groundbreaking Labor women like Senator Susan Ryan devoted themselves to trying to explain this problem with the intention of fixing it . Well it is certainly fixed now , and it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the " woman problem " . Women supporting the Greens are another more recent twist . The gap stands however you measure it . There is a 10-point gap in gender differences within the Liberal Party vote . 45 per cent of men but only 35 per cent of women support the Liberals . 37 per cent of women and 34 per cent of men , a three-point gap , support Labor . The reason that gap is not bigger is that the Greens , whose overall vote is smaller , have a bigger gender gap . 15 per cent of women and 9 per cent of men support the Greens , a gap of 6 per cent which is as stunning as the Liberal gap but in the reverse direction . Combining Labor and the Greens , 52 per cent of women vote centre-left while , combining the Liberals and Nationals , 38 per cent of women vote centre-right . The 10-point gap still holds up . The survey does n't pick up any gender differences in the Nationals ' support . Furthermore , Cameron and McAllister report , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ scale from left to right , the average position for men is 5.2 ( to the right ) , while the average position for women is 4.8 ( to the left ) . Women have moved left since the 1990s . READ MORE OPINION : Gender differences on issues are now also far greater than they used to be . Once again , the gaps are enormous . The economy dominated men 's thinking but not women 's ( for 32 per cent of men managing the economy was the biggest issue but that was the case for only 17 per cent of women ) . Health was front of mind for women ( 30 per cent ) but much less so for men ( 14 per cent ) . On these issues the gender gaps are in the order of 15-16 per cent and therefore even larger than for voting . Now for the second big division , the generational divide . Cameron and McAllister report that in party voting terms older voters are moving further to the right while younger voters are moving further to the left . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ even more stunning . While there has been an age gap favouring the Liberals at many recent federal elections according to the AES ( 2007 was the most recent exception ) , last year was the biggest on record . 55 per cent of voters over 55 voted Liberal compared to just 32 per cent who voted Labor . Even when the Greens ' minuscule 3 per cent is added in , the gap between the Liberals and a vote for the centre-left is a massive 20 points . At the same time , younger people are deserting the centre-right in droves . Only 23 per cent of 18- to 34-year-olds voted Liberal , while a combined 65 per cent voted centre-left ( Labor 37 per cent and Greens 28 per cent ) . That makes a " super-massive " 42 per cent difference . Combining age and gender , the gap would be even greater between younger women and older men . The Greens have a problem to be addressed too , with a miserable 3 per cent of the older vote compared with 28 per cent of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ report , but gender and age differences are enough for now . Old men did beat young women , and these differences are reflected in the composition of political leadership too . Women make some difference in the Senate , but political leadership is now basically wall-to-wall men . That has always been the tendency , but it is now at a high point . Scott Morrison , Michael McCormack , Josh Frydenberg , Anthony Albanese , Richard Marles and Adam Bandt . No Julie Bishop or Tanya Plibersek . Not even Bridget McKenzie . And you can throw in the Governor-General , David Hurley . Older men rule . This report measured dramatic falls in support for Scott Morrison 's leadership and rises in support for making climate and environment action a major issue . These elements are also covered in some detail in the AES election survey , so the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ far on gender and age differences . The parties must decide whether to concentrate on their demographic strong points or do something about their obvious weaknesses . The next election is a long way away , but the parties should already be thinking . To remain in office , the Morrison government must hold on to the support of older men . Have these men been discombobulated enough by the bushfire season and the response of the government to change their vote ? If they have , the attitudes of younger people , especially women , become even more crucial . Until then , old men beat young women . As the eminent economist Ross Garnaut shows in his recent book Superpower , on the new road rural Australia will still be well positioned to keep digging minerals and shipping them overseas . Hydrogen gas , for example , will be a major energy input for industries around the world . Unsurpassed solar resources in areas such as rural Queensland make Australia an ideal source for this new fuel -- unless the Nationals stand in the way . <p> Much of the growth , jobs and cost of living improvements will be concentrated in the rural regions that are most hard-hit by the changing climate and the fading of the old industries -- unless the Nationals stand in the way . <p> All Australians should be concerned about the costs of policy choices for their fellow citizens . The problem with the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be fixated on only a fraction of them . If they are genuinely concerned with jobs and the cost of living , they will help Australia -- and especially rural Australia -- grasp these opportunities . This is the leadership Australia needs . <p> Loading <p> This is also the leadership that the " quiet politicians " in the Coalition , who have for the first time begun breaking that silence , need . Nothing about the Coalition 's values is inconsistent with strategic action on climate change , as conservative British Prime Minister Boris Johnson 's commitment to zero emissions by 2050 shows . <p> When the old road is crumbling , it is standing in the way of the new one that brings the greatest risks . As Dylan wrote , he who is hurt will be he who has stalled . So , National Party , please lend a hand in building the new road . If you ca n't , then get out of Australia 's way . <p> Alan Schwartz is a capitalist , philanthropist , impact investor and founder of the Universal Commons Project @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the London School of Economics and chief economist at the Universal Commons Project .

@@71696752 <p> Every society rests on a web of norms , institutions , policies , laws and commitments to those in need of support . In traditional societies , such obligations are borne mostly by families and kin groups . In advanced economies , a greater share of the burden is placed on the state and markets ( through health insurance and pensions ) . Yet even in the latter case , much of the social contract is still upheld by families ( through unpaid care work ) , civil society ( voluntary and charitable organisations ) and employers ( through benefits they 're required to provide to their employees ) . <p> The social contract is not synonymous with the welfare state . Rather , the welfare state refers to the dimensions of a social contract that are mediated through the political process and subsequent state action , either directly through taxation and public services or indirectly through laws requiring the private sector to provide certain benefits . As such , the welfare state is best understood not as a redistribution mechanism , but as a source of productivity and protection over the course of a person 's life @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has shown , most people contribute as much to the state as they receive in return . <p> Nonetheless , much of the anger that has come to define politics in the developed world is rooted in people 's sense of having not received what they are owed . Those born into disadvantage feel as though they never had a chance . Those living in rural areas believe that policymakers have overwhelmingly favoured cities . Native-born populations fear that immigrants are receiving benefits before they have paid their dues . Men sense that their historic privileges are eroding . Older people regard the young as ungrateful for past sacrifices , and the young increasingly resent the elderly for straining social-security programs and leaving a legacy of environmental destruction . All of this distrust and animosity is fodder for populists . <p> So , too , are the effects of technological change and globalisation . The integration of global supply chains has delivered huge gains to the middle classes in emerging economies and to the top 1% globally , but it has hollowed out the middle and working classes in advanced @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ advanced economies have had to sacrifice wages or social protections to compete with emerging-market labour , and that these pressures have intensified as capital has become more mobile . Worse , the social mobility that once made inequality politically tolerable has stalled or declined . <p> In principle , the provision of adequate insurance against economic displacement should make the pressures from technological change and globalisation manageable . But many aspects of today 's welfare states are still designed for the old economy , where male breadwinners paid into reliable pensions over the course of a lifetime , while women stayed at home to raise children and care for the young and the old . <p> For the first time in history , there are now more women in higher education than men around the world . Educated women have fewer children , are more likely to be in paid work , and will increasingly feel tensions between their participation in the labour market and their traditional caring responsibilities . Yet recent research from the International Monetary Fund shows that closing the gender gap has significant benefits for growth . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ contract so that women can make full use of their talents without any loss of social cohesion . <p> In advanced economies , this tension is at the centre of debates about childcare and declining birthrates . Societal ageing means that a shrinking working-age population must cover rapidly rising healthcare and pension costs . Worse , today 's working-age population already has less security than previous generations , owing to the decline of defined-benefit pensions and a lack of access to many employment benefits or training opportunities . <p> Likewise , climate change represents a breakdown of the intergenerational social contract . Over the past year , young people staged massive protests against an economic model that does n't take adequate account of the environment . As the evidence of an impending climate disaster mounts , so too has support for alternative economic models that would enable more sustainable development . <p> Once we have acknowledged these global challenges , we can begin to envision what a new social contract might look like . For example , education will need to occur earlier in life , when the foundation for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to meet the demand for reskilling . It also will need to focus on tasks that complement what robots can do . Serious investments in reskilling -- on the order of 1 -- 2% of GDP , as in Denmark -- must be central to any modernised social contract . <p> A new social contract also may need to provide a minimum income for all , but structured in a way that preserves the incentive to work and retrain . Earned income tax credits , mandatory training and work placements , and employment guarantees should all be considered . And to tap into the world 's growing pool of female talent , large investments will be needed to expand childcare and eldercare , provide shared parental leave , and counter the effects of formal and informal biases that place women at a disadvantage . For example , if benefits were made portable and provided pro rata , more workers would be able to rely on part-time work to balance other commitments . <p> As for sustainability , we need to adopt an entirely different way of thinking about ageing and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to have any chance of supporting an ageing population , the investments needed to boost future productivity must be made now . In the meantime , ageing populations may have to commit to working longer -- with retirement ages pegged to life expectancy -- and demanding less medicalised health care at the end of life . Finally , current and future environmental costs will have to be incorporated into economic decisions . We need massive investments in green technologies to transform cities , transportation and energy systems . Considered together , such a new social contract has the potential to restore a sense of hope and optimism about the future .

We are on track for at least 3 ? C of warming . <p> But the real worry is that it 's beginning to appear as though the interactions between climate hazards and their cascading impacts are a far bigger threat than we realised . They may ultimately be more severe than the immediate impacts . <p> We 've seen recent indications of that in this summer 's bushfires , where an unprecedented drought combined with record temperatures directly contributed to the destruction of more than 11 million hectares , with cascading impacts such as hazardous air quality affecting millions of Australians ; a 75% increase in Australia 's annual emissions of greenhouse gases ; at least a $4.5 billion blow to Australia 's tourism industry ; and severe losses of wildlife and biodiversity . These local governments are now in the unsustainable situation of chronically recovering from disasters . <p> Nothing but a transformation in Australia 's disaster resilience will prepare us for the increasing scale and frequency of climate hazards and the wide-ranging impact they will have on society . This transformation should start with land-use planning , which is the most important mitigation measure for preventing future disaster losses in areas of new development . Generally , information about bushfire , flood or cyclone risk is not readily available to individuals purchasing homes or businesses making investment decisions . This is a market failure that will increasingly put Australian communities at risk . The disclosure of disaster risk information should be required upon the sale or lease of property and legislation should be enacted giving homeowners the right to know about their property 's exposure to hazards . <p> These measures should be incorporated in the prime minister 's proposal to establish an enhanced national accountability framework for disaster risk management with ' targets , key actions , enhanced national standards and greater transparency ' . <p> Incorporating them would also reinforce similar efforts by financial regulators to ensure that firms and financial institutions understand and transparently disclose their climate-related financial risks to investors , lenders , insurers and other stakeholders . @@71699234 <h> The original paleo diet included seafood with 22 times the safe limit of toxic metals , study finds <p> Stone Age humans may have consumed toxic amount of heavy metals in their seafood , according to a recent study . <p> Researchers found levels of lead 3-4 times in cod and seal were higher than considered safe by today 's standards . Levels of cadmium , another heavy metal , were 15-22 times higher than considered safe , high amounts of mercury were also found . <p> These results suggest that natural food sources may have been unsafe for our ancestors , in part due to climate change . <p> When most people think of the paleo diet , they picture a simple , back-to-basics eating style full of real food like grass-fed meats , sustainable seafood , and some fruits , veggies , seeds , and nuts . <p> What they do n't imagine is a bunch of toxic metals , including lead and mercury -- but that 's exactly what researchers found in a new study on the seafood diet of early humans in Norway , published January 28 in Quaternary International . <p> Researchers from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 40 samples of skeleton remains of Atlantic cod and harp seal , both food sources for prehistoric humans , from eight archaeological sites in a region called Varanger in northeastern Norway . The bones were between 3,800 to 6,200 years old , representing a period of the Stone Age where humans in that region ate mostly seafood , along with some reindeer , beaver , hare , and occasionally some species of birds . <p> They found that evidence that both species contained toxic heavy metals cadmium and lead , in dangerous quantities . The amount of cadmium was between 15-22 times higher than what today considered safe for human consumption ; the amount of lead was between three and four times higher than considered safe . <p> Researchers also found elevated levels of mercury , another toxic heavy metal , although not beyond what is currently regarded as safe . <h> High levels of toxins made Stone Age seafood ' unhealthy if not unsafe , ' researchers concluded <p> All three types of heavy metals found in the seafood remnants are linked to human health issues . Exposure to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , while both lead and mercury can cause brain damage and even death , according to the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention ( CDC ) . <p> Researchers concluded , based on these findings , that " marine food during the Younger Stone Age in Varanger was unhealthy if not unsafe , " according to the study . <p> However , it 's not clear from the data in this study what the health effects of eating contaminated seafood may have been , or even if our Stone Age ancestors lived long enough to suffer the side effects of the toxins . <h> Climate change may have played a role in the level of toxins in seafood <p> In trying to account for these results , researchers found a correlation between the surprisingly high levels of toxins and markers of climate change such as sea surface temperature and shoreline levels . They found that the higher levels of metals , at least in Atlantic cod , were linked to rising sea levels and sea temperatures , potentially due to erosion and/or volcanic activity . <p> However , this study @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ across more bone samples and a broader region , to better understand how changing temperatures and rising seas may have affected our ancestors ' food sources and health .

@@71700684 <h> Opinion <h> In the post-Holden era , we can be a nation of clever designers <h> By Jesse Adams Stein <p> February 20 , 2020 -- 11.45am <p> Much has been said in recent days about General Motors ' axing of the Holden brand . A great deal of this discussion has been about Australian manufacturing , with predictable amounts of finger-pointing . But it was 2017 when GM ceased manufacturing Holden on Australian shores . <p> The termination of Holden in 2020 is not really about manufacturing . The jobs lost this time are in design and sales -- and Holden 's last gasp this year marks a significant historical moment for Australian industrial design . <p> Time piece ... the FJ Holden . Credit:National Museum of Australia <p> This is not to grandstand about some kind of iconic Australian style that is now lost . That 's not what is at stake here . <p> Historically speaking , Holden 's design culture was unique , but not because of chrome curves or sleek fenders . It was unique because of how it drew from a highly skilled Australian workforce of designers and tradespeople . Collaboration was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from a design and engineering partnership between the US and Australia . <p> Advertisement <p> Prior to GM Holden 's 1948 release of its first " all-Australian " car , the nation 's role in automotive design was very limited . Australia was a place for assembly ; the creativity tended to happen in England , France and the US . The injection of Chifley government funding -- alongside the high-quality training provided by technical institutes such as the Working Men 's College ( later RMIT ) -- changed this dynamic . A design culture that fused creativity with trade skills emerged . <p> Loading <p> In my research I have interviewed Australians who worked in manufacturing pre-production from the 1950s to the early 2000s , such as automotive clay-modellers , industrial model-makers , designers and engineering pattern-makers . Until recently , clay-modelling was a widespread method for developing the industrial design form of a vehicle 's chassis . <p> Perfecting the surface of a car involves a deep understanding how light bounces off form , and clay-modellers and designers at Holden co-operated to get this just right . They @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ feel for errors with the lightest touch of a fingertip . <p> Some workers told me that the design culture at Holden was distinctive . " Ford 's very engineering-driven , whereas Holden is design-driven , " said Scott Murrells , a former clay-modeller with experience at both firms . The word he most often used to describe his work at Holden was " creative " . <p> Holden 's design legacy matters because it broadly represents what has happened to Australian industrial design following de-industrialisation . Such shutdowns affect not only manufacturing . In today 's world of offshored and largely digitised production , Australian industrial design offers far fewer opportunities for face-to-face knowledge sharing between designers and tradespeople . To our detriment , we are on the cusp of losing a generative fusion of innovation and practical know-how . <p> Loading <p> The end of Holden represents the risks to innovation when we allow our country to rely on other places for production , when we devalue trades training , and when we rely too much on the market to dictate what will happen to industries and skills @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : pay more attention to local design and rethink how it could be nurtured . <p> Australia still has a chance to excel in well-designed recycled plastic products , which would also be a convenient transformation of our plastic waste problem . But the market can not be left alone to make this happen . History tells us that excellence in design and manufacturing requires targeted government support , not only for industry , but also for skills training , at tertiary and trade levels . <p> It is worth remembering that the idea of an all-Australian car emerged during the Depression and was brought into sharp relief by World War II . In the context of war shortages , and with the need to employ a large post-war workforce , the notion of designing and producing Australia 's own motor vehicle made political and economic sense . <p> Today , as we begin to grapple with volatile markets due to climate change , global disease control and international trade tensions , the need for self-sufficiency may again become salient . <p> Loading <p> This does not mean Australia should @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be front and centre in a drive to produce things that make sense for our own time . <p> A lack of political will has meant that Australia may have missed the opportunity to be a global leader in the electric vehicle industry , for example . <p> By scare-mongering about Labor 's 50 per cent EV target during the last election campaign , the government demonstrated a lack of confidence in what could have been a booming Australian industry . What other opportunities might we miss if we continue to devalue design and skilled trades ? <p> Jesse Adams Stein is a senior lecturer and chancellor 's postdoctoral research fellow at the UTS School of Design , and chief investigator for the Reshaping Australian Manufacturing oral history project , undertaken with the National Library of Australia .

@@71700934 <h> The High Price of Greenwashing <p> ( Bloomberg ) -- Sign up to receive the Green Daily newsletter in your inbox every weekday . <p> In the new age of sustainability , there are plenty of companies pledging to offset emissions in the race for net zero . While certainly an improvement over past years when a pledge to do 10% better was the standard , the trend has triggered skepticism that greenwashing is really what 's at work . Soon , however , there wo n't be anyplace left to hide , especially for companies that quietly use lobbying to keep climate regulation at bay . Late last year , a group of investors with $6.5 trillion in assets under management asked 47 of the world 's biggest greenhouse gas emitters to align their climate efforts with the Paris Agreement 's climate goals . And that was just the beginning . <p> " These mixed messages threaten our collective ability to avoid catastrophic climate change , " Adam Kanzer , head of stewardship for the Americas at BNP Paribas Asset Management , said at the time . Shareholder proposals seeking disclosure of corporate lobbying tend to spike @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ proposals are focused on whether corporate interests are undercutting efforts to fight global warming . Companies that say they are planning to go carbon neutral , but still spend millions of dollars to fight climate legislation , may face some serious backlash when their conflicts are revealed . <p> In the oil and gas sector , the annual climate lobbying spend of the five largest public companies is $201 million , according to InfluenceMap , with an additional $195 million for climate positive branding . BP , which has fought carbon taxes and supported diluted federal reviews of its environmental impact , proclaimed last week that it would look at lobbying as part of a new net zero plan . The oil giant says it plans to " stop corporate reputation advertising and redirect resources to active advocacy for progressive climate policies . " The details of how this company -- part of an industry largely responsible for the climate crisis -- will accomplish such goals have yet to be revealed . <p> The investment industry is n't escaping scrutiny , either . While asset managers pledge to push clients @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ raise money for climate deniers . @@71700996 <p> Shape-shifting bodies . Cracking voices . Hairs sprouting in new places . Puberty marks a dramatic period of change for young people . Now new research shows children who grow up in poor homes enter puberty early . <p> Not only do they experience more emotional , behavioural and social problems compared to their peers , early puberty puts them at risk of a range of health issues for the rest of their lives . <p> The research , published today in the journal Pediatrics , adds to a body of work showing the cumulative effect of adversity in childhood can have lifelong physical , mental and behavioural repercussions . <p> However , the reason why these disadvantaged children enter puberty early remains unclear . And work is continuing to pinpoint factors that trigger the cascade of hormones that mark this critical period of development . <p> Not only do they experience more emotional , behavioural and social problems compared to their peers , early puberty puts them at risk of a range of health issues for the rest of their lives . <p> Puberty is an inherently awkward transition in which a child 's body matures to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with breast development between the ages of eight and 13 and ends with menarche , or the first period . In boys , puberty begins between ages nine and 14 , on average , starting with growth of the sexual organs and wrapping up with facial hair and a deepened voice . <p> But changes at puberty are not all physical . Puberty also triggers rapid biological and social change , and increasing risk for psychological health problems , like depression and anxiety , substance use and abuse , self-harm and eating disorders . <p> We still do n't know exactly what triggers the cascade of hormone secretions that , over time , produces these tell-tale changes . And " What triggers puberty ? " was one of the 125 questions posed in Science magazine 's 125th anniversary edition in 2005 that still remains unanswered today . <p> Other researchers have linked early puberty with living with a stepfather or having experienced stressful life events , such as childhood maltreatment and abuse . <p> In particular , we still do n't know exactly what causes some children to enter puberty @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ linked to early puberty . <p> The stereotype of a ' homeless person ' needs to be eliminated - this is why <p> People who self-identify as ' homeless ' have poorer wellbeing than others in the same circumstances , yet that 's the label they must adopt to qualify for help . <h> What we did <p> Previous studies looking into social impacts on the timing of puberty have had mixed results . While one Indian study found poor girls started their periods later than normal , a UK study found girls who grew up the poorest were twice as likely to have started their periods earlier than the richest . <p> So , we carried out the first study of its kind in Australia to see how cumulative exposure to social disadvantage affected the age children entered puberty . <p> We asked parents of 3,700 children in the Growing Up in Australia Study to report signs of their children 's puberty at age eight to nine , and then again at ten to 11 . Signs included : a growth spurt , pubic hair and skin changes ; @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and facial hair in boys . <p> Girls with early first periods become women with greater risk of gestational diabetes <p> The average age for a girl 's first period has dropped from 17 to 13 years over the past century , and the shift has come with some implications for long-term health . <p> We then compared the family 's socioeconomic position -- as measured by their parent 's annual income , education and employment -- of those who started puberty early with others who started on time . <p> At 10-to-11 years old , about 19 per cent of boys and 21 per cent of girls were classified in the early puberty group . In other words , they had entered puberty earlier compared to their counterparts . <p> Boys from very disadvantaged homes had a four-fold increase in the rate of early puberty , while girls ' risk increased nearly two-fold compared with kids that came from the richest families . <p> What we do know , however , is early puberty is linked with a range of health issues . <h> How could this happen ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ adversity , like extreme poverty , can permanently set the body 's stress response to high alert , affecting the brain 's circuits . This might , in turn , influence how reproductive hormones are regulated , so affecting the timing and trajectory of puberty . <p> Another body of research suggests the social environment can influence so-called epigenetic changes in our genes . These changes might affect the regulation of genes involved in reproductive development , switching some on or off sooner than usual . <p> Another theory is that in the face of hardship -- for instance , economic disadvantage , harsh physical environment , the absence of a father -- children may be programmed to start the reproductive process earlier to ensure their genes are passed on to the next generation . <p> Yet , we still do n't know exactly how poverty or disadvantage triggers early puberty . <h> Why this matters <p> What we do know , however , is early puberty is linked with a range of health issues . <p> For instance , in girls , it 's linked with emotional , behavioural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ substance disorders , eating disorders and earlier-than-usual displays of sexuality . <p> Early puberty also affects people 's health far beyond their teenage years . @@71701598 <h> Pursuit home <h> How do we protect our unique biodiversity from megafires ? <p> Australia 's season of bushfires shows us just how easily our unique biodiversity and ecosystems could be wiped out . Now is the time for long-term planning for climate change to protect them <p> By Professor Ary Hoffmann , Dr James Camac and Nicholas Bell , University of Melbourne <p> Share selection to : <p> This summer 's devastating Australian fires and their continuing impact on biodiversity serve as a stark reminder of the challenges in nature conservation as we head into an increasingly volatile future driven by climate change . <p> It is no longer sufficient to protect land areas as part of a national reserve system in the hope that these areas can protect the rare and vulnerable species within them and maintain overall biodiversity . <p> The continuing impact of Australia 's bushfires on biodiversity remind us of the challenges in nature conservation . Picture : Getty Images <p> Megafires destroy vast tracts of land and are now occurring at a frequency and severity that prevents natural ecosystem recovery processes . <p> While scientific evidence has highlighted that most Australian ecosystems @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the occasional severe fire , the increase in frequency and severity is likely to result in substantial and permanent impacts . <p> Across a timeframe of hundreds of thousands of years , biodiversity has persisted in natural environments despite substantial shifts in climate as a result of evolutionary processes that allows it to adapt to any gradual changes in climate . <p> The increase in bushfire frequency and severity is likely to result in permanent impacts on Australia 's ecosystem . Picture : Getty Images <p> At a genetic level , these refugia also typically harbor high levels of genetic variation both within and between species . Important genetic refugia are well known in the northern hemisphere , including some North American trees , where they have been identified in relation to glaciation ( the formation , movement and recession of glaciers ) . <p> Identifying key biodiversity refugia within a landscape is no easy task . <p> This is because locations with high species richness are not always the same locations as those that are capable of buffering against environmental change while also maintaining high genetic diversity . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with the better tools to identify locations which have acted as refugia for thousands of years . <p> These particular refugia , called evolutionary refugia , highlight areas where populations have persisted though substantial environmental change and where genetic connectedness has provided an influx of new genetic material . <p> The highly endangered Mt Donna Buang wingless stonefly ( Riekoperla darlingtoni ) . The larvae of the species have only been found in three small mountain summit populations within a three kilometre radius of the mountain . Picture : Eddie Tsrylin <p> The groups in these refugia , both related and unrelated , often show overlapping patterns of genetic diversity -- showing us that conserving evolutionary refugia can protect biodiversity across multiple organisms . <p> For instance , refugial areas of native insects in Victoria 's alpine region have been found around mountain summits . But other organisms , including plants , show similar patterns of high genetic diversity . <p> While the exact reasons these patterns exist may remain unclear , they highlight areas where disparate species have persisted despite major environmental changes . <p> Modern DNA approaches have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ evolutionary history . <p> We can now can track ancient changes in population size as well as unpick how organisms have moved in and out of refugial areas . These tools have become cheaper and more readily available , allowing us to build up detailed pictures of persistent diversity across our landscape . <p> Following the devastating fires this summer , now is the time to identify , conserve and protect genetic refugial areas . <p> We need to plan for extra protection measures in identified biodiversity refugia ; we 've already seen it 's possible to protect key areas in times of crisis after specialist firefighters were deployed to save the world 's last stand of ancient Wollemi Pine from the Gospers Mountain fire in New South Wales . <p> The devastating extent of the 2003 fires in the Victorian Alpine region . Picture : Henrik Wahren <p> The trees ' preservation means , in the long term , that they can be used as source populations when , or if , the climate stabilises . <p> But , in the short term , it 's critical we ensure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by promoting the movement of individuals with diverse genotypes across the wider landscape . <p> This means human involvement -- distributing seed , eggs and other propagules . It is important to move away from local management of environments to ' evolutionary ' management of biodiversity that recognises that the entire landscape can not be preserved . <p> We need to rethink biodiversity protection and take a much longer perspective in terms of its conservation , accepting that we can not ' save ' species , but that we can only reduce the extent to which biodiversity is depleted . <p> This requires strong leadership , political will and an evolutionary approach to conservation as our climate changes . <h> Privacy Statement <p> The University of Melbourne ( University ) collects , uses , handles and discloses personal information in accordance with the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 ( Vic ) ( Act ) and other applicable legislation . <p> This Privacy Statement relates only to the collection of personal information in relation to the Pursuit Website . @@71701716 <p> After the United Kingdom voted in 2016 to leave the European Union , policymakers and political leaders across Europe feared that they too would soon face a similar crisis . They worried about a domino effect in which populist movements and politicians would lead other member states out of the EU one by one , effectively reversing a decades-long process of European integration . <p> But , at least until recently , Brexit had the opposite effect . Much to everyone 's surprise , the EU in the years after the UK 's referendum enjoyed a Brexit dividend . Europeans watched the UK descend into political chaos , with Britons literally stockpiling food and medicine for fear of what the future might hold . EU member states that typically agree on very little suddenly found themselves united behind the European Commission 's negotiating strategy . Support for the EU among Europeans soared . Until 31 December 2020 , British companies will continue to have full access to the EU single market , Britain will remain in the customs union , and British citizens will be able to travel freely across Europe . <p> So far , then , the real-world costs of Brexit have been essentially nil . @@71701723 <h> Australians ' relationship with their country -- secrets and lies <p> How can you engage with Australians when evidence shows we lie to our families , friends and even ourselves ? <p> Unexpected election results around the world including most recently in Australia -- despite polling suggesting otherwise -- is just one factor suggesting there is a gap between what people say publicly , and what they actually believe . Understanding these factors is important to be able to develop effective policies , products , services and communications to drive behaviour change . <p> A 2019 study from WPP AUNZ , Secrets and Lies , is helping to fill this knowledge gap . The Mandarin recently sat down with Rose Herceg , chief strategy officer for WPP AUNZ and author of the study , to understand more . <p> The study kicked off around 18 months ago and combined a large sample of 4,500 Australians and 1,500 New Zealanders with individual interviews to dig deep into the psyche . The sample selected was representative of the population with respect to diversity , gender , socio-economic status , and location . <p> Delivered in three chapters , chapter one @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at national identity and chapter three at how over 55s view themselves and how they want to live their lives vs their perceptions of the way they are treated and the things they are offered . <p> In a twist to conventional research , Dr Michael Henderson , a leading anthropologist studying human behaviour and motivation , was engaged to cast an anthropological lens across the results . Through all this , with anonymity guaranteed , people were encouraged to open up about how they really feel about their lives and the world they live in . <p> According to Rose , this study has brought home to WPP the restrictions of conventional research in delivering actionable results that will drive change . The methodology enabled a conversation where subjects could safely open up and express their true thoughts . <p> For example , there was a woman deeply regretting motherhood despite initially saying it was the most important thing in her life ; a person living in a loveless marriage ; a person using his private bank accounts to purchase drugs ; an HIV positive subject who had not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ voter in the same sex marriage plebiscite . <p> Revealing the real ' quiet Australians ' <p> The results revealed 49% of Australians misrepresent themselves . Out of the respondents , 52% had lied at work , 63% had made up an excuse to get out of a social arrangement , and 70% regularly told white lies to spare a person 's feelings . <p> This is despite the fact that 81% value the idea of living an authentic life . <p> " The notion of measuring the difference between the things you are really thinking , and the things you let yourself say out loud , is not just interesting , it can lead to a whole different interpretation of the results and therefore what you do with them , " Rose said . <p> In the world of politics , 66% of Australians said they do n't feel they are adequately represented . " A lot of the feedback is for the government to get on with it -- whether that is climate change , small business or roads . People want to know where all of the innovative ideas are to get this done from what has been discussed in the many white papers . " <p> Where Australians dramatically differ in what they say and think is on the topic of equality -- with Herceg explaining the uncomfortable truth for Australia is we only want to pretend we 're all equal . <p> " On a national level we are very good at the fa ? ade , " Herceg said . " <p> For Australia , this is one of the nation 's big national secrets -- the fact that we tell the world we 're equal , we help our mates and love our nature . But the reality is that most Australians do not want to support others if it risks disadvantaging themselves . The recent bushfire crisis , coupled with the ongoing drought , of course , point to the fact that Australians will rally around in a crisis , but in general times Australians are less motivated by a desire for true equality than a desire to ward off personal disadvantage . <p> Communicating to Australians <p> The results of the research have highlighted for Herceg that motivation and behaviour is driven by three factors : protection , privacy and power . @@71703982 <p> Using DNA sequencing on ancient pack rat nests made of plants , insects , bones , fecal matter and urine could give us a look into Earth 's past , according to research published Thursday in the journal Ecology and Evolution . The study could help scientists better understand how plant communities , as well as potentially animals , bacteria and fungi , will react to climate change . <p> " Rodent middens are powerful tools in paleoecology , " Michael Tessler , a postdoctoral fellow at the American Museum of Natural History , said in a statement . " We wanted to see how we could take this invaluable resource and expand its use to give us a big-picture view of what life in the Americas was like 1,000 , 10,000 , or even 30,000 years ago , and measure how it has changed in the time since then . " <p> Pack rats are nocturnal rodents that use plant materials to build nests in dry caves . Their urine helps to hold the nests together . This allows the nests to be preserved for tens of thousands of years , with some dating to before the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ limited foraging range , their middens are made up of contents representative of the local environment at the time the materials were collected . This could give us clues about previous environments and climates , the study says . <p> " Midden contents are so well preserved that fragments of ancient DNA can be extracted and analyzed across millennia , " Rob Harbert , an assistant professor at Stonehill College , said in the statement . " They have been used to identify an extinct ground sloth preserved in southern Argentina , tell us about the history of bighorn sheep in California , and provided evidence of papillomavirus infection in packrats over the last 27,000 years . " <p> Fossil middens throughout the Americas could allow us to " genetically profile entire communities through time and space , " Harbert added , but we first need to improve how we analyze data from the deposits -- a key goal of the study . <p> Researchers analyzed DNA from 25 pack rat midden samples ranging from 300 to 48,000 years old , which came from City of Rocks National Reserve in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Scientists focused on a sequencing technique for comparing DNA , called shotgun , that randomly chooses DNA fragments to sequence . They found that pack rat middens as old as 32,000 years have recoverable DNA consistent with fossils found in the deposits . <p> Because the shotgun technique sequences random bits of DNA , researchers need to have a solid database to match the sequences to an organism . If there is n't any data for that organism , they 'll only get either the nearest match or no match . This , in addition to DNA degradation , allowed researchers to definitively match the DNA fragments only to the family level , and not to genus or species groupings . <p> " As the costs of DNA sequencing continue to decrease and computational power increases , the prospects for using this technique will greatly improve , " Harbert said . " Further investigation into the taxonomic composition of middens could refine our understanding of the timeline of past climate change , species migration , and extinction , and this will better inform the study of the effects of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @

These are known as pyroCbs , or simply firestorms . <p> A pyroCb event occurs when a fire is sufficiently large and intense to create a plume which punches up to and even into the stratosphere , taking with it smoke , ash , heat , water and quite probably causing wind storms , cold downdrafts , lightning , even the uncanny black hail which Canberra residents in 2003 found so disturbing . <p> Not many years ago , pyroCbs were quite rare , an interesting , if scary , scientific curiosity . <p> At a fire weather conference in Bowral , NSW , in 2011 , Dr Mike Fromm of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory told me that he had been on a research flight in a NASA DC8 when , high in the troposphere @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fittings , he said , but gum leaves . <p> He was smelling the smoke from an Australian bushfire . @@71704992 <h> Forests , logging and climate change <p> THE INTERGOVERNMENTAL PANEL for Climate Change ( IPCC ) recommends that " natural solutions " are employed to deal with climate change emergency . The immediate protection and restoration of natural systems for carbon dioxide removal ( CDR ) are preferred to geo-engineering and B.E.C.C.S -- burning biomass as a fossil fuel substitute while using some sort of carbon capture and storage . <p> It is clear that the resilience of natural systems must be enhanced to withstand climate change impact , lest they falter and collapse , inhibiting their capacity for CDR . <p> The fairytale that burning wood instead of coal is carbon neutral continues to wreak havoc on the world 's extant forests . But that fairytale could soon end , taking with it the myth that the industrial logging of the world 's native forests has been and is now " sustainable " . <p> For a long time , the falsity of carbon emission accounting for forest bioenergy has been apparently invisible to many policymakers . These emissions can not be re-captured by tree regrowth within the timeframe required to prevent irreversible global warming . This is the decade in which emissions must be radically cut , while atmospheric CO2 is simultaneously drawn down from the atmosphere -- if we all want to survive . <p> It could take up to 100 years before new plant growth might re-sequester the carbon emitted from the wood burning . That 's especially the case when it comes to climate denial . <p> The paper -- which has n't yet been peer-reviewed or published yet -- zoomed in on May 28 to June 31 , 2017 . That covers the period immediately preceding and after U.S. President Donald Trump 's announcement he was going to withdraw the U.S. from the Paris Agreement on June 1 . All told , the analysis turned up some 6.5 million tweets using terms such as " climate change , " " global warming , " and " Paris Climate Agreement . " To narrow their analysis of who was real and who was n't , the researchers chose a random sample of roughly 167,000 tweets to analyse . <p> To identify media bots @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or sway public opinion -- the researchers Botometer , a university-led effort that rates social media accounts for authenticity . Turns out that bots were n't posting as much around the Paris Agreement announcement because more actual people had climate change on the mind . But among the content that the bots were most interested in amplifying was climate denial . <p> You know , tweets promoting fake science claiming that the climate crisis is n't real or research the fossil fuel industry has funded to help keep its business growing despite the risks to humanity . Bots , on average , had a 0.5 per cent greater chance of tweeting about denialist research . And overall , bots accounted for a quarter of all climate tweets , suggesting these fake accounts are a big part of #climatetwitter . And it 's concerning that climate denial , in particular , is more likely to be pushed by Twitter bots . <p> " One of the most dangerous elements of misinformation is its ability to cancel out accurate information , " John Cook , a researcher at the Centre for Climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the study , wrote in an email to Earther . " When people are exposed to both facts and myths , if they have no way of resolving the conflict between the two , then they disengage and the two cancel each other out . This is what makes misinformation from bots so dangerous . Misinforming tweets do n't need to be especially convincing or successfully persuade people -- its mere existence is all that 's needed to reduce the effectiveness of accurate information . " <p> And a Twitter bot could very well fool anyone who might not have the surest grasp of climate science or spotting misinformation in general .
